'''Richard K. Yamamoto''' (1935–2009)<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://news.mit.edu/2009/obit-yamamoto|title=Richard Yamamoto, physics professor, dies at 74|last=Trafton|first=Anne|date=October 16, 2009|newspaper=MIT News|access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref> was an American [[elementary particle]] [[physicist]] and professor of physics at [[MIT]] focusing primarily on the study of [[Lepton|leptons]] and quarks and their interactions. To this end he was involved with experiments at Brookhaven, Fermilab, and [[SLAC]], including the [[BaBar Experiment]]. He was also known for his expertise in building experimental hardware, which he shared with students.

== Biographical information and education ==
Richard K. Yamamoto was born June 29, 1935, in [[Hawaii]], the son of Richard M. Yamamoto, a service station proprietor, and Yatsuko Yamamoto, a waitress.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://interactive.ancestry.com/2442/M-T0627-04584-00875?pid=82671885&backurl=//search.ancestry.com//cgi-bin/sse.dll?_phsrc=aBY10&_phstart=successSource&usePUBJs=true&gss=angs-g&new=1&rank=1&msT=1&gsfn=Richard%2520K.%2520&gsfn_x=0&gsln=Yamamoto&gsln_x=0&MSAV=1&msbdy=1935&cpxt=1&cp=12&catbucket=rstp&uidh=ro8&pcat=ROOT_CATEGORY&h=82671885&dbid=2442&indiv=1&ml_rpos=8&treeid=&personid=&hintid=&usePUB=true&_phsrc=aBY10&_phstart=successSource&usePUBJs=true#?imageId=M-T0627-04584-00874|title=1940 U. S. Census, Honolulu, Hawaii|date=April 9, 1948|website=interactive.ancestry.com|access-date=December 27, 2016}}</ref> He became a freshman at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) in 1953, earning an A.B. in 1957 and a Ph.D. in 1963,<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Fisher|first=Peter|title=Obituary of Richard Yamamoto|journal=[[Physics Today]]|doi=10.1063/PT.4.1510|year=2010 |issue=7 |article-number=3031 |bibcode=2010PhT..2010g3031F }}</ref> working with advisor Irwin A. Pless.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=211371|title=Physics Tree: Richard Kumeo Yamamoto|date=January 27, 2016|website=The Academic Family Tree|access-date=December 27, 2016}}</ref>

He was known to enjoy working with his hands. A practiced mechanic and a devotee of fast cars, he rebuilt his own car engines and took driving lessons at [[NASCAR]] tracks.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/fnl/volume/224/yamamoto.html|title=In Memoriam: Richard K. Yamamoto|website=web.mit.edu|publisher=MIT Faculty Newsletter|access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref>

With his first wife Lily, a [[graphic designer]],<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://winchester.wickedlocal.com/news/20160113/winchesters-book-ends-to-host-author-of-stina|title=Winchester's Book Ends to host author of 'Stina'|date=January 13, 2016|newspaper=The Winchester Star|access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref> Yamamoto had three daughters and eight grandchildren.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=SJ&p_theme=sj&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&s_dispstring=allfields(Richard%20Yamamoto)%20AND%20date(2009)&p_field_date-0=YMD_date&p_params_date-0=date:B,E&p_text_date-0=2009&p_field_advanced-0=&p_text_advanced-0=(%22Richard%20Yamamoto%22)&xcal_numdocs=20&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&xcal_useweights=no|title=Richard Yamamoto|date=October 27, 2009|via=nl.newsbank.com|work=[[San Jose Mercury News]]|access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref> His second wife, Kathleen (Cougan) Barreto (1955-2012)  was from [[Sunnyvale, California]], and had a career in [[Silicon Valley]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/mercurynews/obituary.aspx?n=kathleen-barreto-yamamoto&pid=157341493|title=Kathleen Barreto-Yamamoto's Obituary on Mercury News|date=April 29, 2012|newspaper=[[San Jose Mercury News]]|access-date=December 28, 2016}}</ref>

Yamamoto died October 16, 2009, of complications related to [[lung cancer]].<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Yamamoto spent his entire career at MIT, first as a researcher at the Laboratory for Nuclear Science in 1963, and as an instructor in 1964.<ref name=":0" /> In 1965 he became an assistant professor, and in 1972 a full professor.<ref name=":0" /> His colleague [[Edmund Bertschinger]] said, "His kindness and gentle enthusiasm helped make the department an exciting and supportive place for everyone in physics."<ref name=":1" />

Yamamoto loved teaching, both in the classroom and in the laboratory.  For many years he taught the Junior Lab at MIT, as a master of all the experiments.<ref name=":2" />

== Research ==
Yamamoto conducted research at three national laboratories: [[Brookhaven National Laboratory|Brookhaven]], [[Fermilab]], and [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]].<ref name=":0" /> At Fermilab, was credited with "a leading role in the creation, operation, and exploitation of the 30-inch [[Bubble chamber|Bubble Chamber]] Hybrid [[Spectrometer]] in studying [[hadron]]ic interactions".<ref name=":0" /> In the SLD collaboration at SLAC, he studied Z0 [[boson]] production and decay in polarized electron-positron collisions, measuring "the electroweak mixing angle based on a polarized electron-positron scattering".<ref name=":0" /> Yamamoto's group contributed a "precise measurement of the electron beam polarization based on [[Compton scattering]]".<ref name=":0" /> The MIT faculty newsletter described it as "the most precise measurement of the [[Electroweak interaction|electroweak]] mixing angle (sin2θW) based on a single process".<ref name=":2" /> That measurement was "an important constraint on models of electroweak symmetry breaking, including the possible mass of the [[Higgs boson|Higgs Boson]] in the [[Standard Model]]".<ref name=":2" />

[[File:Yamamoto-Junior-Lab.jpg|thumb|left|Yamamoto in lab with magnetic spectrometer]]

Colleagues have said his [[management style]] was low-key, yet effective. Colleague [[Peter H. Fisher|Peter Fisher]] began working in 1994 with Yamamoto. Fisher said, "He loved to work with students, making things...He was happiest when he had his hands on some knob, adjusting a mirror, and looking at an [[oscilloscope]]."<ref name=":1" /> Fisher commented, "Dick was a mild-mannered guy, but when push came to shove, he stood up to the system." Fisher described a situation at SLAC when the Center's director was pressuring Yamamoto's team to publish their results, even though the team members were puzzled why two different electron-counting methods produced different results. Yamamoto insisted that they needed to know why the numbers were off, and they only published when they figured it out.<ref name=":1" />

His group also "conducted precise studies of decays of charmed and bottom particles" at the [[BaBar experiment|BaBar]] [[B-factory|B-Factory]].<ref name=":0" /> He was involved in creating the BaBar drift chamber, contributing to measurement of [[CP violation]] and properties of heavy [[meson]]s.<ref name=":0" /> One source commented, "He was happiest building something and making it work. Many of his students have gone on to careers in physics and carry with them his love of experimental hardware."<ref name=":2" />

== Honors, awards ==

* 2008 winner of MIT's "Infinite Mile Award"<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.mit.edu/policies/infinite-mile-previous-winners#2008|title=MIT School of Science Infinite Mile Award Previous Winners|date=2008|website=science.mit.edu|access-date=December 31, 2016}}</ref>
